title: Rubella Infection in Children
subject: Paediatrics
summary: Rubella is a mild viral exanthem that can cause serious congenital defects if acquired in pregnancy. Diagnosis relies on clinical features and serology, while management is supportive and focused on prevention through vaccination.

sections.p: Rubella is an acute, self‑limiting infection caused by the rubella virus, a togavirus transmitted by respiratory droplets.
b: Clinical case definition: fever <38.5 °C, maculopapular rash lasting 3 days, posterior auricular and occipital lymphadenopathy.
Laboratory confirmation: rubella IgM positive or a four‑fold rise in IgG in paired sera.

t.b: Detects recent infection; a positive result confirms diagnosis in the acute phase.
Shows seroconversion; a four‑fold rise confirms recent infection when IgM unavailable.

t.a: RT‑PCR on throat swab or urine
t.b: Detects viral RNA; useful in outbreak settings or when serology is equivocal.

sections.p: Rubella is usually mild (stage 1). Severe disease is rare but may occur in immunocompromised children or in congenital rubella syndrome (CRS).
b: Stage 1: uncomplicated exanthem with low‑grade fever.
Stage 2: arthralgia, thrombocytopenia, or encephalitis (very rare).
Stage 3: congenital rubella syndrome – multi‑system disease in neonates.

sections.p: Rubella virus infection acquired via respiratory droplets; outbreaks are common in settings with low vaccination coverage.
b: Community outbreak in schools or clinics (most common).
Nosocomial spread in crowded wards.
Maternal infection during pregnancy leading to CRS.

sections.p: The child typically presents with a brief fever, tender posterior auricular/occipital lymph nodes, followed by a pink maculopapular rash that starts on the face and spreads downward over three days.
b: Mild conjunctivitis without copious discharge.
Occasional mild arthralgia in older children.
Rare complications: encephalitis, thrombocytopenia.

sections.p: In low‑resource settings, rely on clinical picture and basic serology; advanced tests may be unavailable.

t.b: Confirms recent infection; if unavailable, treat as probable case based on clinical criteria.
Detects thrombocytopenia; a low platelet count may signal severe disease.

t.b: Screens for CRS‑related anomalies when serology is positive.

sections.p: Complications are uncommon but must be recognised promptly.
b: Encephalitis – altered consciousness, seizures.
Severe thrombocytopenia – petechiae, bleeding.
Congenital rubella syndrome – cataracts, deafness, cardiac defects.

sections.p: No specific antiviral therapy; care is supportive and preventive.
b: Fever control with paracetamol; avoid aspirin in children.
Hydration and rest; monitor for bleeding or neurological change.
Educate caregivers on isolation for 7 days from rash onset.
Vaccination of susceptible contacts with measles‑rubella (MR) vaccine after 6 weeks of illness resolution.

sections.p: Ensure complete recovery and prevent future outbreaks.
b: Re‑examine after 1 week to confirm rash resolution and absence of complications.
Screen pregnant women for rubella immunity; give MR vaccine to non‑immune women after delivery.
Maintain high community vaccination coverage (≥95 %).
Measles – higher fever, Koplik spots, cough, coryza.
Scarlet fever – sandpaper rash, strawberry tongue, positive strep test.
Roseola (HHV‑6) – rash appears after fever resolves, typically in infants.

sections.p: Serology may be falsely negative early or cross‑react with other togaviruses.
b: IgM may be negative if drawn <5 days after rash; repeat testing after 7 days.
Vaccination within the past month can produce transient IgM positivity.

whenToSeekHelp: Suspected congenital rubella in a newborn.

faq.q: Is rubella dangerous for the child?
faq.a: In most children it is mild and self‑limiting; danger lies mainly in pregnant women and rare complications.

faq.q: Can I give aspirin for fever?
faq.a: No; use paracetamol to avoid risk of Reye’s syndrome.

faq.q: When is the MR vaccine given in Kenya?
faq.a: At 9 months in targeted areas, often together with yellow‑fever vaccine.

exam: What clinical features differentiate rubella from measles? — Look for low fever, posterior auricular nodes, and a 3‑day rash without cough or Koplik spots.
A child presents with fever, rash, and thrombocytopenia. How do you confirm rubella? — Perform rubella IgM; if unavailable, treat as probable rubella and repeat serology after 7 days.
Why is aspirin contraindicated in a child with rubella? — It increases risk of Reye’s syndrome, a potentially fatal hepatic encephalopathy.
A pregnant woman reports a rash 2 weeks ago. What is your next step? — Test for rubella IgM/IgG; if positive, arrange fetal ultrasound and counsel on CRS risk.
In a low‑resource ward without serology, how would you manage a suspected rubella outbreak? — Isolate cases, provide supportive care, and vaccinate susceptible contacts after the outbreak resolves.
What are the red‑flag signs that require urgent referral? — Encephalitis, severe thrombocytopenia, or bleeding, and suspicion of CRS in a newborn.
Explain why the MR vaccine is preferred over separate measles and rubella vaccines in Kenya. — Combined schedule reduces visits, improves coverage, and aligns with the national immunisation program.
How does congenital rubella syndrome present at birth? — Cataracts, sensorineural deafness, cardiac defects (e.g., PDA), and growth retardation.
